about: A file's protection mark (a chat's `secureContext: true`), as ONE grammar both sides implement: src/lib/frontmatterBlock.ts `protectionMark` and src-tauri/src/protection_mark.rs `marked`. src/lib/protectionMarks.test.ts and the Rust tests in protection_mark.rs (and corpus_write_lane_tests.rs, for a native note read) run every case below. Seventh review of pull request 267: TypeScript and Rust disagreed, so a protected chat written one way reopened unmarked on the other side. Where the grammar can't be sure, it says marked.
grammar: 1. Lines are split on \n; one trailing \r is dropped from each. One leading byte-order mark is ignored.

2. Blank (empty or whitespace-only) lines before the opening fence are skipped. The first other line, with trailing whitespace removed, must be `---`; otherwise the file has no block and is not marked.
3. The block is the lines after that fence up to the first line that, with trailing whitespace removed, is `---`. A block that never closes can't show the mark absent: marked.
4. A block line names the key when it has a colon and the text before the first colon, trimmed, is the key, at any indentation (an indented key may be a nested one; that is unsure, so it counts).

5. Its value is the text after that colon, trimmed, with one pair of surrounding quotes removed, compared case-insensitively. `false`, `no` and `off` are a clear no. Anything else (true, TRUE, yes, empty, unknown) marks.
6. Any line that marks marks the file, even when another line for the same key says no (duplicate keys).

cases.name: a byte-order mark before the fence
duplicate keys, the last says no
duplicate keys, the first says no
the words in the body, not the block
